adj:pseudonym.tx: Borrowed from French pseudonyme (“pseudonymous”, adjective), from Latin pseudōnymus (adjective), from Ancient Greek ψευδώνυμος (pseudṓnumos, adjective, literally “having a false name”), from ψευδής (pseudḗs, “false”) + ὄνῠμᾰ (ónŭmă, dialectal form of ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”)) + -ος (-os, adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, pseudo- + -onym.

adv:pseudonym.tx: Borrowed from French pseudonyme (“pseudonymous”, adjective), from Latin pseudōnymus (adjective), from Ancient Greek ψευδώνυμος (pseudṓnumos, adjective, literally “having a false name”), from ψευδής (pseudḗs, “false”) + ὄνῠμᾰ (ónŭmă, dialectal form of ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”)) + -ος (-os, adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, pseudo- + -onym.

adj:parallel.tx: Borrowed from Latin parallēlus, parallēlos, from Ancient Greek παράλληλος (parállēlos).

adj:power.tx: Borrowed from French pauvre, from Latin pauper.

noun:Parlament.tx: Inherited from Middle High German parlamënt n (“meeting; disputation; assembly”), from Old French parlement (“parliament”), from Middle English parlement (“discussion; parliament”), itself from Old French parlement (“discussion”), from parler (“to speak”) + -ment, from Medieval Latin parabolō (“to speak”).

noun:Python.tx: 17th century, learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Πύθων (Púthōn). In the biological sense since 19th century.

adj:plan.tx: From Middle High German plān, from Latin plānus.

adj:proper.tx: Ultimately from Old French propre, from Latin proprius. Probably borrowed in north-western dialects via Middle Dutch proper [13th c., sense: 15th c.], later generalized under the influence of modern French propre. The colloquial euphemism for “chubby” may, in part, be due to association with Proppen (whence also proppenvoll and Wonneproppen).

noun:Pflanze.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German pflanza, borrowed from Latin planta. Cognate with Hunsrik and Luxembourgish Planz. Doublet of Clan.

verb:pflanzen.tx: From Middle High German pflanzen, from Old High German pflanzōn. Cognate with Hunsrik planze, flanze. By surface analysis, Pflanze + -en.

noun:Präsident.tx: From French président, itself from Latin praesidens. First attested in the 16th century.

noun:Pharao.tx: Learned borrowing from Late Latin Pharaō.

prep:per.tx: From Late Middle High German per (15th c.), from Latin per, in part through Italian per.

noun:Pfund.tx: From Middle High German pfunt, phunt, from Old High German pfunt, phunt, from Proto-West Germanic *pund, from Proto-Germanic *pundą, a borrowing from Latin pondō (“by weight”, adverb) or Latin pondus (“weight”, noun).

intj:prost.tx: Contraction (early 18th c.) of prosit (16th c.), from Latin prōsit (“may it be beneficial”). Originally used as a blessing in various contexts, e.g. as a polite response to sneezing. Remnants of such freer use are prost Mahlzeit and prost Neujahr. Compare Dutch proost.

verb:plagen.tx: From Middle High German plāgen (“punish”), from Late Latin plagare (“hit, wound”); see also Plage. Cognate with English plague, Dutch plagen, Spanish plagar.

adj:prompt.tx: From French prompt, from Latin prōmptus (“visible, apparent, evident”), past participle of prōmō (“to take or bring out or forth, produce, bring to light”), from prō (“forth, forward”) + emō (“to take, acquire, buy”). Doublet of Prompt.

adv:prompt.tx: From French prompt, from Latin prōmptus (“visible, apparent, evident”), past participle of prōmō (“to take or bring out or forth, produce, bring to light”), from prō (“forth, forward”) + emō (“to take, acquire, buy”). Doublet of Prompt.

noun:Panzer.tx: From Middle High German panzer, panzier, from Old French panciere (“coat of mail to protect the belly”), from pance (“paunch, belly”) (compare Medieval Latin panceria, pancerium), from Latin pantex (“paunch, belly”). See also Pansen.

adj:proportional.tx: Proportion + -al, from Latin prōportiōnālis. Doublet of proportionell.

adj:perplex.tx: Borrowed from French perplexe, from Latin perplexus.

verb:pinkeln.tx: From Pinkel, originally meaning "pinky finger, penis".

adj:pathogen.tx: From πάθος (páthos, “suffering, pain”) + -γενής (-genḗs, “producer of”). Equivalent to patho- + -gen.

noun:Paar.tx: From Middle High German par, from Old High German par, from Latin pār.

noun:Pack.tx: From Low German pack, from Middle Low German pak, from Old Saxon *pakko, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô. Akin to, and possibly borrowed from, Dutch pak.

noun:Palette.tx: Borrowed from French palette, diminutive of pale (“shovel, blade”), borrowed from Latin pāla (“spade, shoulder blade”).

noun:Palisade.tx: Borrowed from French palissade, from Old Occitan palissada, palissa. Ultimately from a derivative of Latin pālus. See also Pfahl.

noun:Pampa.tx: Borrowed from Spanish pampa, from Quechua pampa (“plain, prairie”).

noun:Pantheon.tx: From Ancient Greek Πάνθειον (Pántheion, “a temple of all gods”).

noun:Papier.tx: From Middle High German papier, from Old French papier.

noun:Paprika.tx: Borrowed from Hungarian paprika, from Serbo-Croatian pàprika, from pȁpar, from Proto-Slavic *pьpьrь, from Latin piper, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”), from Sanskrit पिप्पलि (pippali, “long pepper”).

noun:Park.tx: A doublet of inherited Pferch (“pen [for animals]”). The form Park was first borrowed in the 15th/16th centuries from Middle Dutch park, in which the word had developed the sense “recreation park, enclosed hunting grounds” under the influence of Old French parc. German Park remained sporadic, however, until it was reinforced (or borrowed anew) from modern French parc and English park from the …

noun:Party.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English party. Doublet of Partei and Partie.

noun:Pass.tx: From Early New High German pass, from Middle High German pas (“parts of a deer's entrails”) (but also West Central German "step, walk, gait, way", also "the right measure; the right, appropriate time" by influence of Middle Dutch, whence Late Middle High German pas (“"measured part, section”), compare the verb passen). Borrowed from Old French pas (“pace, step”) (partially intermediated by Middle …

noun:Passion.tx: Borrowed from Latin passio, partially through French passion.

noun:Pate.tx: From Middle High German pate, bate, from Medieval Latin pāter spīrituālis. Compare Middle Low German pāde, Old High German pate (“godmother”), Middle High German pfetter (from Old High German pfetiro (“godfather”)). Related to German Pfetter.

noun:Patience.tx: Late 18th century. Formally from French patience, but the use for a card game is apparently older in German than in French and English.

noun:Patina.tx: Borrowed from Italian patina. Doublet of Patene and Patine.

noun:Patriot.tx: Borrowed from French patriote, from Late Latin patriōta, from Ancient Greek πατριώτης (patriṓtēs).

noun:Patron.tx: From Middle High German patrōn, from Latin patrōnus. Doublet of Patrone.

noun:Pause.tx: From Middle High German pūse, borrowed from Middle French pause (14st), from Latin pausa.

noun:Pedant.tx: Borrowed from French pédant (literally “schoolmaster”), from Italian pedante, from Ancient Greek παιδεία (paideía).

noun:Pelle.tx: From Middle Low German *pelle, whose existence is assured by the word’s prevalence in eastern dialects of German Low German (and East Central German). It was introduced there by Dutch settlers from Middle Dutch pelle, an old borrowing from Latin pellis (“skin”). Compare modern Dutch pel, pellen.

noun:Pension.tx: Borrowed from French pension, ultimately from Latin pēnsiō, pēnsiōnem.

noun:Perineum.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin perinaeum, from Ancient Greek περίναιον (perínaion).

noun:Perle.tx: From Middle High German perle, from Old High German perala, perula, from Vulgar Latin *perla (compare Old French perle). Further origin uncertain; perhaps from perna (“leg”), referring to the shape of the bivalve. See pearl for more.

noun:Person.tx: From Middle High German persōn, persōne.

noun:Pest.tx: 16th century, from Latin pestis, in part through Middle French peste. Popular shortening of Middle High German pestilencie (14th c.), from related Latin pestilentia, may also have contributed (though this is impossible to prove).

noun:Petition.tx: From Latin petītiō (“a request, petition, beseeching”).

noun:Phalanx.tx: 16th century, learned borrowing from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx), in part through its descendant Latin phalanx.

noun:Phantom.tx: Borrowed from French fantôme, from Old French fantosme, from Latin phantasma, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma).

noun:Phase.tx: 18th century, apparently a back-formation from Phasen, the plural of former common and now obsolete Phasis, influenced by French phase. Ultimately from Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “appearance”), from φαίνομαι (phaínomai, “I appear”) + -σις (-sis). Doublet of Phasis.

noun:Phrase.tx: Borrowed from Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).

noun:Piano.tx: Borrowed from Italian piano which was clipped from pianoforte, from Latin plānus.

noun:Pietà.tx: Borrowed from Italian pietà, from Latin pietās.

noun:Pike.tx: From Middle High German pieke, from Middle Dutch pike, from Old Dutch *pīk, from Proto-West Germanic *pīk. Already in Dutch the word was influenced by French pic (“tip”). Another influence is German Picke (“pick, pickaxe”), from picken. The precise relation between all of these words is uncertain.

noun:Pilot.tx: Ca. 1500, from Italian pilota, in part through Middle French pilote.

noun:Pint.tx: From Middle High German pint, from Middle Low German pint, from Old Saxon *pint, from Proto-West Germanic *pint(i). Cognate with English pintle and German Low German Pint.

noun:Pipi.tx: Euphemistic reduplication of Pisse, perhaps after French pipi.

noun:Plage.tx: From early Middle High German plāge, from Latin plāga (“blow, wound”). The word was originally chiefly Central German, therefore sometimes secondarily adapted to the Upper German consonantism as (later) Middle High German pflāge, which form did not last, however. More at plague.

noun:Plan.tx: Borrowed from French plan. Compare Hunsrik Plaan.

noun:Plane.tx: From Middle High German blā, blahe, from Old High German blaha, from Proto-Germanic *blahwǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlok-. The modern form is East Central German with intrusive -n- (taken from the Middle High German genitive-dative blān, blahen) and sporadic p- for initial b-. Related with Icelandic blæja (“veil”). Not related with plan (“planar, flat, smooth”), though it may be associated with it.

noun:Planet.tx: From Middle High German plānēte, a loanword from Latin planeta, planetes, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs), a variant of πλάνης (plánēs, “wanderer”). The German term Wandelstern is a calque of the former.

noun:Plankton.tx: Derived from Ancient Greek πλαγκτός (planktós, “drifter”), from πλάζω (plázō, “I turn aside, wander”). Coined by German zoologist Victor Hensen in 1887.

noun:Plasma.tx: From Late Latin plasma (literally “mold”), from Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “something formed”).

noun:Plunder.tx: From Middle High German plunder (“household furniture, clothes, linen”). Cognate with Middle Low German plunde (“clothing”), Dutch plunderen (“to plunder”).

noun:Plural.tx: From German Pluralis, from Latin (numerus) plūrālis.

noun:Plutonium.tx: Borrowed from English plutonium, hence from Pluto in the sense of the dwarf planet.

noun:Po.tx: Clipping of Popo, a 17th-century reduplication of the first syllable of Podex, from Latin pōdex.

noun:Poet.tx: From Middle High German poēte, from Latin poēta, from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs, “creator, composer”).

noun:Pogrom.tx: Borrowed from Russian погро́м (pogróm). First attested in the late 19th century, in more general use since the Russian pogroms of 1905.

noun:Poker.tx: Borrowed from English poker, itself perhaps derived from German Pochspiel (pochen + Spiel).

noun:Pol.tx: From Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos) via Latin polus.

noun:Pole.tx: From Middle High German *Pole or *Polen (attested as Polen m pl), from Old Polish polanín, from Proto-Slavic *poľaninъ (literally “field-dweller”), derived from *pȍľe (“field”). The Middle High German form may have been a strong noun in -en in light of polnisch; the weak form is then a backformation (cf. Heide, Rabe etc.).

noun:Pollen.tx: Borrowed from Latin pollen. Common since the 18th century, occasionally already Middle High German bolle, Old High German polla.

noun:Poller.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Poller, from early modern Dutch polder (“bollard”), itself via Middle French [Term?] and/or Middle Dutch [Term?] from Old French poltre (“beam”). Compare contemporary Dutch bolder, modern French poutre, and possibly English bollard.

noun:Polymer.tx: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πολυμερής (polumerḗs, “consisting of many parts”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + μέρος (méros, “part”).

noun:Pomp.tx: From Middle High German pomp(e) f (13th c.), from Old French pompe and directly from its source, Latin pompa, which see. Masculine use began in the 15th century and established itself by the 18th.

noun:Pony.tx: Late 18th century, from English pony. Until the earlier 20th century often masculine; the neuter was reinforced by analogy with Pferd n.

noun:Popo.tx: A 17th-century childish reduplication of the first syllable of Podex, from Latin pōdex. Probably also influenced by nursery language, as common with such terms.

noun:Portal.tx: From Old French portal and/or Medieval Latin portāle.

noun:Position.tx: From Latin positiō. Cognate with Hunsrik Posizion.

noun:Post.tx: Borrowed from Italian posta, from posto, from Latin positus. Doublet of Pfosten and Posten.

noun:Premier.tx: Borrowed from English premier and French premier. Doublet of primär.

noun:Prior.tx: Inherited from Middle High German prīor, from Latin prior.

noun:Prise.tx: Ca. 1400, from Middle French prise (“spoils”), from prendre (“to take”). The monophthongal form and the restriction to nautical context probably established themselves under influence of Middle Low German prîse, from the same source. The diphthongised form is preserved in preisgeben (“to surrender, relinquish”). The sense “pinch” (18th c.) is a renewed loan from Modern French.

noun:Probe.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin proba, from the classical Latin verb probāre.

noun:Professor.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin professor (“declarer, person who claims knowledge”).

noun:Profil.tx: Borrowed from French profil and Italian profilo.

noun:Profit.tx: 16th-century borrowing from German Low German profit, borrowed in turn around 1400 from Lower Rhine Middle Dutch profijt, from Old French profit, porfit (“advantage, profit, benefit”), from Latin prōfectus (“progress, growth, knowledge”), from prōficiō (“to advance”).

noun:Promotion.tx: From Late Latin promotio, from Latin promoveo (“to move forward”).

noun:Propaganda.tx: 18th century, short for Latin Congregatio de propaganda fide, a papal missionary committee. The modern use since the mid-19th century after French propagande, at first in left-wing parlance.

noun:Prophet.tx: Borrowed from Latin prophēta, from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs).

noun:Proportion.tx: Borrowed from French proportion, from Latin prōportiō.

noun:Protein.tx: Suggested by Berzelius in a letter to Mulder, from Ancient Greek πρωτεῖος (prōteîos, “primary”), from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”), with a suffix derived from Latin -īnus.

noun:Protest.tx: From Italian protesto. Originally used in a merchant context, such as in refusing a bill of exchange. The modern usage was influenced by protestieren.

noun:Psalm.tx: Relatinized form of older Salm (now an informal doublet meaning “lengthy talk”), from Middle High German salm(e), from Old High German salmo, from Latin psalmus, which see for more. The spelling ps- is occasionally attested also in Old and Middle High German, though this need not reflect an according pronunciation. The form was spread chiefly through Luther’s Bible. Dialectally, the pronunciation …

noun:Pseudonym.tx: Borrowed from French pseudonyme (“fictitious name”, noun), a coinage from pseudo- + -onyme (noun-forming suffix) inspired by the Ancient Greek adjective ψευδώνυμος (pseudṓnumos). Compare Contemporary Latin pseudōnymum.

noun:Psi.tx: From Ancient Greek ψεῖ (pseî), the name for the twenty-third letter of the Greek alphabet (Ψ, ψ (Ps, ps)).

noun:Pullover.tx: Borrowed from English pullover with a spelling pronunciation.

noun:Puma.tx: 18th century, from Spanish puma, from Quechua puma.

noun:Pute.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German *pūte, imitative of the bird’s (mating) call. Compare German put (with a short vowel), a word used to call chickens and other farm birds (DWDS).

noun:Putsch.tx: Borrowed from Alemannic German Putsch (literally “blow”), popularized in the context of the Züriputsch in Zurich (1839).

noun:Porree.tx: Borrowed from Middle French porrée, from Latin porrum.

verb:pissen.tx: From northern Middle High German pissen and Middle Low German pissen, by surface analysis, Pisse + -en. Perhaps borrowed through Middle Dutch pissen from Old French pissier, from Vulgar Latin *pīssiāre, probably of echoic origin, though the Germanic words are also sometimes considered independent onomatopoeias.

verb:piesacken.tx: From a Low German dialectalism Ossenpesek (literally “ox pizzle”) from Pese (“tendon”), Peserik (“rod”), as a pizzle was used in the 18th century to beat man and animal.

noun:Pfanne.tx: From Middle High German pfanne, from Old High German phanna, from Proto-West Germanic *pannā, from Proto-Germanic *pannǭ, from Late Latin panna, from Latin patina (“bowl, platter”). Doublet of Patina.

noun:Pfannkuchen.tx: From Pfanne (“pan”) + Kuchen (“cake”). Cognate to Low German Pannkauken (“pancake”).

noun:Pfannkuchengesicht.tx: From the association of the form of a face with the form of a pancake.

noun:Platin.tx: Borrowed from French platine, from Spanish platina.

verb:pfeifen.tx: From Middle High German pfīfen, from Old High German pfīfōn, from Proto-West Germanic *pīpōn (“to play a flute; to whistle”). Cognate with Hunsrik peife, Yiddish פֿײַפֿן (fayfn).

adj:plump.tx: From Middle Low German plump, itself onomatopoeic for a dull fall (as of a stone into water, or a sack on the ground). Cognate with Dutch and Middle Dutch plomp (13th c.), whence also English plump. Alemannic German has shifted forms in Alsatian pflumpfig, Swiss pflumpfet, but these were probably formed analogically as the word moved up the Rhine (and thus do not prove West Germanic inheritance).

noun:Pilates.tx: Probably a variant of Pilatus, which occurs as an (also rare, but slightly more common) surname.

noun:Partei.tx: From Middle High German partīe, from Old French partie. Cognate with English party, Italian partita. Doublet of Partie and Party.

adj:platt.tx: From northern Middle High German plat, blat and Middle Low German plat, from Old French plat, from Vulgar Latin *plattus, probably from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús). Compare Dutch plat, French plat, Italian piatto, obsolete English plat. Also related to English flat.

noun:Pech.tx: Inherited from Middle High German pëch, bëch, from Old High German pëh, bëh, from Proto-West Germanic *pik (“pitch, tar, wood resin”), from Latin pix. The form is unusual as it shows unshifted p-, but shifted -ch, even though the shift of initial p- to pf- occurred later than that of postvocalic -k to -ch. Theodor Frings therefore considered that the word was at first restricted to West Central …

noun:Punkt.tx: From Middle High German punct, Late Latin pūnctus. Doublet of bunt.

adj:pünktlich.tx: From Punkt + -lich. Further from Latin punctus (p.p.p. of pungō), whence also English point, punctual. Compare typologically Russian то́чный (tóčnyj) (akin to то́чка (tóčka), ты́кать (týkatʹ)).

noun:Pappel.tx: From Medieval Latin papulus (“poplar tree”), a variant of classical Latin pōpulus; compare Dutch peppel (from Middle Dutch pappel).

noun:Preiselbeere.tx: Preisel- + Beere. The former part of the word is borrowed from Upper Sorbian bruslica.

noun:Präzision.tx: From French précision, from Latin praecīsiō.

noun:Prostata.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōstata, from Ancient Greek προστάτης (prostátēs, “one standing before, protector”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

noun:Pinkepinke.tx: Reduplication of Pinke of the same meaning, from criminal slang and of unknown origin.

adj:pur.tx: From Late Middle High German pūr (14th c.), from Latin pūrus.

noun:Pumpe.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German pumpe, pompe, from Middle Dutch pompe. Further origin uncertain, but probably onomatopoeic. Compare English pump.

intj:pfui.tx: From Middle High German pfui, phiu, probably imitative of spitting out.

noun:Pelz.tx: From Middle High German pellez, from Old High German pelliz, from Latin pellīcia. Cognate with English pelt, Vilamovian pełc.

noun:Perl.tx: From French perle (“pearl”), used by Jean Jannon for the type used in his miniature editions of Horace, Vergil, and the New Testament in the 1620s.

noun:Pimmel.tx: Cognate with Dutch piemel (“penis”). The further origin is uncertain. Closely related to Dutch piemelen (“to pee, water”) alongside dialectal pingelen, German pinkeln. These are likely onomatopoeic, but can also be compared to Dutch pink (“pinkie, little finger”), Low German Pink (“penis”). A further connection is made with Low German pümpeln (“to thrust, bump”), to which belong German pimpern …

noun:Phönix.tx: Relatinization of Middle High German fēnix, fēnichs, fēnīs, themselves (in part through Old French fenix) from Latin phoenix, from Ancient Greek φοῖνιξ (phoînix).

noun:Pferd.tx: From Middle High German phert, phærît, pherit, pferift (“riding horse”), from Old High German pherit, pfarifrit, parafred, from Proto-West Germanic *parafred, from Late Latin paraverēdus (originally “substitute post horse”). Largely displaced the native word Ross. Compare Dutch paard and English palfrey.

verb:pimpern.tx: Probably borrowed from Low German pümpern (“to crush in a mortar”), from Middle Low German pumpen (“to beat, thump”). Compare Pimmel.

noun:Pasch.tx: From the earlier dialectal paschendise, from French passe-dix (“passage”), name of a game of chance using dice.

noun:Pfeffer.tx: From Middle High German pfëffer, from Old High German pfëffar, pfëffur, from Proto-West Germanic *pipar (“pepper”).

noun:Pfütze.tx: From Middle High German pfütze, from Old High German pfuzzi, from Proto-West Germanic *puti (“a well”). Doublet of Pütz (“well; bucket”) and Pütt (“mine shaft”).

noun:Pilz.tx: Regional form with initial b → p and unrounding, from Middle High German bülez, bülz, from Old High German buliz, from Proto-West Germanic *bulit (“porcini”).

verb:passieren.tx: Borrowed from French passer. Compare English pass.

noun:Pfad.tx: From Middle High German pfat, from Old High German pfad, from Proto-West Germanic *paþ.

adv:partout.tx: 18th century, from French partout (“everywhere”), which has a related use as an intensifier of commandments, especially in nautical parlance. The German sense may have developed thence. Or perhaps from the expression toujours et partout (“always and everywhere, invariably, necessarily”).

noun:Pflug.tx: From Middle High German pfluoc, from Old High German pfluog, phluog, from Proto-West Germanic *plōg, from Proto-Germanic *plōgaz, *plōguz (“plough”). Cognate with Low German Ploog, Dutch ploeg, English plough, Scots pleuch, plou, West Frisian ploech, North Frisian plog, Danish plov, Swedish plog, Icelandic plógur.

noun:Pfand.tx: From Middle High German phant, from Old High German phant. Only found in base form in continental Germanic languages, such as Dutch pand and Swedish pant (though derivatives also exist in insular Germanic as Icelandic panta (“to reserve, order”)), and of unresolved origin, various Latin sources have been suggested: Latin pāctum (“agreement”) under the supposition of a Low Latin *pantum from …

noun:Platz.tx: From Middle High German plaz, from Old French place, from Latin platēa, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), shortening of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”). Cognate with English place. Displaced native Old High German zīh (“place, court/village square, market”).

intj:Platz.tx: From Middle High German plaz, from Old French place, from Latin platēa, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), shortening of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”). Cognate with English place. Displaced native Old High German zīh (“place, court/village square, market”).

noun:Plexiglas.tx: Coined by Otto Röhm in 1933, from Latin plexus (“interwoven”) + Glas (“glass”), equivalent to plexi- + Glas, alluding to polymerization.

noun:Pflaume.tx: From Middle High German pflūme, from Old High German pflūma, from Proto-West Germanic *plūmā (“plum”).

noun:Pfahl.tx: From Middle High German pfāl, phāl, from Old High German pfāl, from Proto-West Germanic *pālu, from Latin pālus.

noun:Pfarrer.tx: From Old High German pfarrāri, from pfarra (“parish”), probably from Late Latin parochia, from Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía).

noun:Pfau.tx: From Middle High German pāwe, pauwe, from Old High German pfāwo, from Proto-West Germanic *pāwō (“peacock, peafowl”).

noun:Pfeife.tx: From Middle High German pfīfe, from Old High German pfīfa, from Proto-West Germanic *pīpā (“flute, pipe”).

noun:Pfeil.tx: From Middle High German pfīl, from Old High German pfīl, from Proto-West Germanic *pīl, from Latin pīlum (“javelin, throwing spear”). Cognate with German Low German Piel, Dutch pijl (“arrow, dart”), English pile (“column of wood, steel or concrete”).

noun:Pfeiler.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German pfīlāri, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *pīlāre, from Latin pīla (“a pillar”). Cognate with Hunsrik Peiler.

noun:Pfingsten.tx: From Middle High German phingesten, from Late Latin pentēcostē, from Ancient Greek πεντηκοστή (pentēkostḗ). The Old High German form fimfchusti is a partial calque of the Ancient Greek term, with πεντη- (pentē-) replaced by fimf (“five”). Cognate with Hunsrik Pingste and Dutch Pinksteren.

noun:Pfirsich.tx: From Middle High German pfërsich, from Old High German phërsih, from Proto-West Germanic *persik (“peach”).

noun:Pflaster.tx: From Middle High German pflaster, from Old High German pflastar (“plaster, pavement”), from Proto-West Germanic *plastr.

noun:Pflege.tx: From Middle High German pflege, probably from Old High German *pflega, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *plegō. Compare the German pflegen (verb).

verb:pflegen.tx: From Middle High German phlëgen, from Old High German plëgan, from Proto-West Germanic *plehan.

noun:Pflicht.tx: From Old High German pfliht, from Proto-West Germanic *plihti. Cognate with English plight, Scots plicht (“responsibility, plight”), Dutch plicht, Low German Plicht (“duty”), Danish pligt (“duty”), Yiddish פֿליכט (flikht).

noun:Pflock.tx: From Middle High German pfloc (late 14th century). Related with Middle Low German plügge (1375, or plugge), also pluck, plock (ca. 1420), Dutch plug (1511 as plugghe, also plogge), all “peg, wooden nail, pin, plug." Probably from the same ultimate source as English plug. Further origin uncertain. The word shows semantic relations with a nominal derivative of Proto-Germanic *plukkijaną (“to …

noun:Pforte.tx: From Middle High German pforte, from Old High German pforta, from Proto-West Germanic *portā (“portal, gateway”), from Latin porta (“gateway, passage”).

noun:Pfosten.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German pfost, from Proto-West Germanic *post (“post, pedestal”). Sense 5 is a semantic loan from English post.

noun:Pfote.tx: From Middle Low German pōte. Cognate with Dutch poot. The onset pf- through secondary and inadequate adaptation to the Upper German consonantism. (The expected form of a hypothetical cognate would be *pfoße.)

noun:Pfropfen.tx: From Middle Low German proppen, prop, borrowed into East Central German and thence into the standard language (early 18th century). The modern form is a secondary adaptation to the Upper German consonantism, based formally on the verb pfropfen (“to engraft”, eventually from Latin propago), which in Low and Central German had the form proppen, thus identical to the unrelated noun. Cognate with Dutch prop.

noun:Pacht.tx: From Middle High German pfaht, from Latin pactum (“pact”). The unshifted onset p-, the feminine gender, and the contemporary plural form in -en are northern influences from German Low German [Term?] and/or West Central German. In Grimm's German dictionary, the word is still treated as a masculine noun with plural Pächte; this is now obsolete.

noun:Peitsche.tx: From a Slavic language (compare Polish bicz, Czech bič), from Proto-Slavic *bičь (“whip, lash”), from *biti (“to beat”) + *-čь.

verb:pflücken.tx: From Middle High German pflocken, pflucken, pflücken, from Old High German phlockōn, *phlucken, from Proto-West Germanic *plukkōn, from Proto-Germanic *plukkōną. Compare Luxembourgish plécken, Hunsrik plicke, Rhine Franconian plicke, plocke, Dutch plukken, English pluck. Within High German the word was restricted to Central German and northernmost Upper German.

noun:Pilger.tx: From Middle High German pilgerīn, bilgerīn, bilgerīm, from Old High German piligrīm, from Proto-West Germanic *pelegrīm (“pilgrim, foreigner”).

noun:Pinsel.tx: From Middle High German pënsel, bënsel, from Old French pincel, from Vulgar Latin pēnicellus, alteration of Latin pēnicillum (“brush”).

noun:Polster.tx: From Middle High German polster, bolster, from Old High German polstar, bolstar, from Proto-West Germanic *bolstr, from Proto-Germanic *bulstraz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“bag, pillow, paunch”). Compare English bolster, Dutch bolster, Swedish bolster.

noun:Pracht.tx: From Middle High German braht, from Old High German braht, from Proto-Germanic *brahtaz.

noun:Preis.tx: From Middle High German, ultimately from Latin pretium.

verb:prüfen.tx: From Middle High German prüeven (13th c.), originally restricted to Central German. Ultimately from Latin probāre and hence a doublet of proben and probieren. The Middle High German form with umlaut (and also Rückumlaut in the past tense pruofte) suggests a Proto-West Germanic *prōfijan, whence also Dutch proeven, Middle Low German prö̂ven. The late attestation on the other hand speaks in favour …

noun:Puder.tx: Borrowed from French poudre. Doublet of Pulver.

noun:Pulver.tx: From Middle High German pulver, from Old High German pulver, from Proto-West Germanic *pulver (“powder”). Doublet of Puder.

noun:Pult.tx: From Middle High German pulpet, from Latin pulpitum.

noun:Puppe.tx: Borrowed from Latin pupa. Sense of "pupa" borrowed from New Latin.

verb:platzen.tx: From Middle High German platzen, blatzen (“to splat, thump, fall noisily”), from plaz, blaz (“splat, thump”), of onomatopoeic origin. Ultimately the same word as platschen (“to splat, splash”) with the development /ts/ > /tʃ/ (as in klatschen, Pritsche, rutschen etc.); the /ts/ is still preserved in Platzregen (“downpour”). Closely related also with Dutch plassen, Middle Low German plasken, English plash.

noun:Prozess.tx: From Middle High German process, borrowed from Latin prōcessus.

noun:Platte.tx: From Middle High German platte, from Old High German platta (ca. 900), from Vulgar Latin *platta, *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “wide; flat”). Doublet of Plätte and Pläte.

noun:Pulsar.tx: Borrowed from English pulsar, a blend of pulsating and star.

adv:plötzlich.tx: From late Middle High German plotzlich, from Plotz (“clap, slap”) (onomatopoeic), originally adverb, since Luther also in adjectival use. By synchronic analysis, from an onomatopoeic element plotz (“sound of a quick impact or blow”) + -lich (“-like”). Cognate with Hunsrik pletzlich. Compare also Middle Low German plutzlik (> Danish pludselig, Swedish plötslig). Related to Early New High German …

adj:plötzlich.tx: From late Middle High German plotzlich, from Plotz (“clap, slap”) (onomatopoeic), originally adverb, since Luther also in adjectival use. By synchronic analysis, from an onomatopoeic element plotz (“sound of a quick impact or blow”) + -lich (“-like”). Cognate with Hunsrik pletzlich. Compare also Middle Low German plutzlik (> Danish pludselig, Swedish plötslig). Related to Early New High German …

verb:posen.tx: From Pose, influenced by English pose (verb).

verb:pulen.tx: Borrowed from German Low German and Middle Low German pulen (“to pull out”), ultimately related to Old English pullian (“to pluck out, pull”).

verb:passen.tx: Borrowed from French passer, intermediated and influenced by Dutch passen. Compare the noun Pass. From Middle French passer, from Old French passer, from Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun).

noun:Prüfung.tx: From prüfen + -ung; cognate with Hunsrik Priefung.

verb:poppen.tx: Regionally attested in the sense “to knock or beat rapidly”, which is probably onomatopoeic. The vulgar sense spread in the 20th century from dialects including Central Franconian, perhaps via film and broadcasting companies based in Cologne. In the latter, the word is sometimes secondarily associated with Popp, cognate and synonym of standard Puppe (“doll”); compare etymology 2. Related with southern Dutch poepen.

noun:Papagei.tx: From Middle High German papegei, from Old French papegai, from Old Spanish papagayo, from Medieval Greek παπαγάς (papagás), from Arabic بَبَّغَاء (babbaḡāʔ). Further origin unknown, perhaps from an African language or imitative. The Middle High German variant papegān may have been borrowed directly from Medieval Greek during the Crusades; compare modern Turkish papağan.

noun:Polizei.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin policia, from Late Latin polītīa.

noun:Punker.tx: From Punk + -er, from English punk, analogous to Rocker.

noun:Primadonna.tx: 18th century, from Italian prima donna (literally “first woman”).

noun:Paranuss.tx: From Para (“Pará”) + Nuss (“nut”), compare dated English paranut.

noun:Petersilie.tx: From Middle High German pētersilje, federscella, from Old High German *petarsilia, federskella, from Proto-West Germanic *petarsilljā, *petarsīlijā.

noun:Pils.tx: Clipping of Pilsener, from Pilsener Bier, that is beer of Pilsen (now Plzeň, Czech Republic), where the manner of brewing was invented.

noun:Papst.tx: From Middle High German pābest, bābest, from earlier bābes, from Old High German bābes, from Old French pape, from Latin pāpa, pappa (“father”, originally). Doublet of Pfaffe. Forms in B- remained predominant during the 15th and 16th centuries before they were gradually displaced by the more Latin-like forms in P-. The contemporary standard spelling was conclusively established by Adelung.

noun:Pistole.tx: Borrowed from French pistole, itself probably via Middle High German pitschal, pischulle from Czech píšťala (“firearm”, literally “tube, pipe”), from Old Czech píščala.

noun:Pentagramm.tx: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πεντάγραμμον (pentágrammon, literally “having five written (lines)”).

noun:Posaune.tx: From Middle High German busūne, busīne, from Old French buisine, from Latin būcina, with a change to stress on the last syllable (influenced by the suffix -īnus).

noun:Pudel.tx: A shortened form of Pudelhund, a compound of Hund (“dog”) and German Low German Pudel, Pūdel (“puddle”), from the onomatopoeic term pudeln (“to splash about”).

noun:Philosophie.tx: From Middle High German philosophīe, from Latin philosophia, which see. Not fully integrated during the Middle High German period; therefore the inherited form in -ei did not establish itself.

noun:Pyramide.tx: 15th century, as Pyramis, from Latin pyramis, from Ancient Greek πυραμίς (puramís). The modern form since ca. 1600 from the Graeco-Latin inflected stem (genitive pyramidis, πυραμίδος), possibly after Middle French pyramide.

adj:porös.tx: Borrowed from French poreux, equivalent to Pore + -ös.

noun:Pirat.tx: Borrowed from Italian pirata, from Latin pīrāta, from Ancient Greek πειρατής (peiratḗs).

noun:Perücke.tx: From French perruque. Further origin uncertain.

noun:Paradies.tx: From Middle High German paradīs(e), from Old High German paradīs, from Latin paradīsum. The modern form with -ie- perhaps partly from non-diphthongising dialects, but chiefly after the Latin.

noun:Papiertiger.tx: Calque of English paper tiger, Papier + Tiger

noun:Palast.tx: From Middle High German palast (13th c.), enhanced form of older palas (12th c.), from Old French palais, from Latin palātium. Doublet of Pfalz, Palas, and Palais. Stress varied until the 19th century (Pálast or Palást).

noun:Pendel.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pendulum, from pendulus (“hanging”), from pendeō (“I hang”).

noun:Pinguin.tx: Early 17th century. Borrowed, perhaps through Dutch pinguïn (1595), from English penguin, which originally referred to the now extinct great auk. Further origin uncertain. Probably either from Welsh pen gwyn (literally “white head”), the great auk having two characteristic white patches near the eyes; or from Latin pinguis (“fat, plump”), referring to the plumpish appearance of both birds. …

noun:Prinz.tx: From Old French prince, from Latin prīnceps (“first head”), from prīmus (“first”) + capere (“seize, take”).

noun:Prinzessin.tx: From Prinzess(e) (“princess”) + -in (redundant female suffix). The former through Middle Dutch princesse from Old French princesse.

noun:Palme.tx: Inherited from Middle High German palme, from Old High German palm, borrowed from Latin palma, from Proto-Italic *pal(a)mā, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂meh₂, from *pleh₂-, possibly from *pleth₂- or *pel-.

noun:Parfüm.tx: Borrowed from French parfum, ultimately from Latin per (“through”) + fūmum, the accusative singular of fūmus (“smoke, steam, fume”).

noun:Pickel.tx: From Old High German *pīk, from Proto-West Germanic *pīk (“pickaxe, sharp point”); + -el.

adj:persönlich.tx: From Middle High German persōnlich. By surface analysis, Person + -lich. Cognate with Hunsrik persenlich, Yiddish פּערזענלעך (perzenlekh).

adv:persönlich.tx: From Middle High German persōnlich. By surface analysis, Person + -lich. Cognate with Hunsrik persenlich, Yiddish פּערזענלעך (perzenlekh).

adj:politisch.tx: From French politique, equivalent to Politik + -isch. Cognate with English politic.

noun:Punsch.tx: Ca. 1700, from English punch, from Hindi पाँच (pā̃c, “five”).

noun:Platten.tx: Short form of German platter Reifen (“flat tire”).

noun:Plastik.tx: Borrowed from English plastic (“malleable, flexible”). Compare Hunsrik Plasdik.

noun:Passwort.tx: From Pass + Wort. In use since Early Modern German meaning a watchword, for which more commonly Parole or Losung. The contemporary use chiefly after English password.

noun:Puls.tx: From Late Middle High German puls, from Latin pulsus.

noun:Profi.tx: Clipping of Professional + -i, first half of the 20th century.

noun:Pappe.tx: From Middle High German *pappe (attested 15th century, but earlier the derivative pepelen, from the source of modern Papp (“thick soup, mash”). Also compare modern päppeln. The original sense of the word was “pap, mush cooked from flour” and “wheatpaste, flour-based glue”. It was then used for a material of book covers made by gluing together several sheets of paper, whence finally “any thick …

noun:Priester.tx: From Middle High German priester, from Old High German priester, borrowed around 700 (after the High German consonant shift, but before the diphthongisation of West Germanic ē) from pre-Old French prestre, from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros). Doublet of Presbyter. Immediately cognate with Dutch priester, Low German Preester, French prêtre. Compare also English …

noun:Prärie.tx: Borrowed from American English prairie, from French prairie.

noun:Prozent.tx: Borrowed from Italian per cento, from Latin per (“through, by”) and centum (“hundred”), modified by the influence of Latin pro (“for”) or German pro.

noun:Passagier.tx: From Middle French passagier (possibly through Middle Dutch), from Old French passagier, derived from passage, itself from passer, from Latin passāre, derived from passus (“a step, pace”). Compare modern French passager, Dutch passagier, English passenger.

noun:Pranger.tx: From northern Middle High German pranger (13th c.), derived from *prangen, a West Central German form of phrengen, phrangen (“to force, squeeze, confine”), from Proto-Germanic *pranganą (compare English prong). Not related with prangen, but possibly at some point associated with it.

adj:pittoresk.tx: From French pittoresque, from Italian pittoresco.

noun:Penisneid.tx: Coined by Sigmund Freud, Penis (“penis”) + Neid (“envy”).

adj:privat.tx: Borrowed from Latin prīvātus. First attested in the 16 century.

noun:Pleite.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish פּליטה (pleyte, “escape, getaway”), via Rotwelsch, 19th c.

noun:Politiker.tx: From Latin politicus with -er for -us; structurally, Politik + -er.

noun:Pförtner.tx: Inherited from Middle High German phortenære, pfortenære, from Old High German portināri, ultimately from Medieval Latin portenarius, from Latin porta. Alternatively analyzable as Pforte + -ner (agentive/job description suffix)

noun:Paradigma.tx: 16th century, from Latin paradigma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma).

noun:Pfalz.tx: From Middle High German phalanze, phalenze, pfalze, from Old High German phalanza, phalinza, falenza, borrowed from Medieval Latin palantia, from palātia, from palātium.

adj:praktisch.tx: From Late Latin practicus, influenced by French pratique.

adv:praktisch.tx: From Late Latin practicus, influenced by French pratique.

noun:Phobie.tx: From words ending in -phobie, from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

noun:Pionier.tx: Borrowed in the 17th century from French pionnier, a soldier employed to form roads, dig trenches, and make bridges, as an army advances.

noun:Pfifferling.tx: Middle High German phefferlinc, Old High German phiferia, related to Pfeffer (“pepper”). In the figurative sense apparently a reference to its (former) ubiquity.

noun:Produktion.tx: Borrowed from French production, from Latin productio, productionem.

adj:populär.tx: From Latin populāris, from Latin populus (“people, nation”).

noun:Popularität.tx: Borrowed from French popularité in the 18th century.

noun:Platine.tx: Borrowed from French platine, from French plat (“flat”).

noun:Programm.tx: From Latin programma (partly through French programme), from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).

verb:pensionieren.tx: Borrowed from French pensionner. Also Pension + -ieren.

verb:planschen.tx: Onomatopoeic origin, compare also platschen, panschen, manschen.

verb:pürieren.tx: Derived from Old French purer, from Late Latin purare (“to clean”).

noun:Prügel.tx: From Late Middle High German brügel, an l-suffixed formation from Middle High German brüge (“framework”), itself related to Proto-Germanic *brugjǭ (“bridge”), with semantic shift "framework" > "structured object" > "club, cudgel".

noun:Projekt.tx: From Latin prōiectum, neuter of the perfect passive participle of prōiciō (“throw forth, extend; expel”). Attested since the mid-17th century.

noun:Persönlichkeit.tx: From Middle High German persōnlīcheit. By surface analysis, persönlich + -keit. Cognate with Dutch persoonlijkheid.

noun:Prozessor.tx: Borrowed from English processor, ultimately from Latin prōcēdō (“to proceed”).

noun:Pampelmuse.tx: Borrowed from Dutch pompelmoes. Further origin uncertain, but the first two syllables are probably—either originally or by secondary association—the dated Dutch noun pompel (“something squat or plump”), to which compare German pummelig. Formerly, the form Pompelmuse was also used; the -a- may be due to influence by French pamplemousse, also from the Dutch.

noun:Primat.tx: From substantive use of Late Latin prīmās (“chief; noble”) (genitive prīmātis), from Latin prīmus (“prime, first rank”) + -ās.

noun:Prognose.tx: 18th century, from Latin prognosis, from Ancient Greek πρόγνωσις (prógnōsis).

noun:Provokation.tx: From Latin provocatio. Attested since the mid-16th century.

noun:Plombe.tx: Borrowed from French plombe, from Latin plumbum.

verb:patrouillieren.tx: 17th century, from French patrouiller. By surface analysis, Patrouille + -ieren.

noun:Pastille.tx: Borrowed from French pastille, from Spanish pastilla, from Latin pastellum, diminutive of pasta (“dough, paste”).

adj:parat.tx: Borrowed from Latin parātus. Compare Dutch paraat.

adj:perfide.tx: Borrowed from French perfide, from Latin perfidus.

noun:Pappmaschee.tx: Borrowed from French papier mâché (literally “chewed-up paper”).

adj:prägnant.tx: Borrowed from French prégnant (“meaningful”, originally “pregnant”), from Latin praegnans (“pregnant”). The sense of the German adjective is not far from the French, but its particulars may have developed under influence of unrelated prägen (compare especially einprägsam).

noun:Pansen.tx: From Middle High German panze, from Old French pance (Modern French panse), from Latin pantex (“belly”).

noun:Pfadfinder.tx: From Pfad + Finder, calque of English pathfinder.

verb:peilen.tx: From German Low German peilen, from Middle Low German peylen, pēgelen, pegelen (“to measure water depth”), from pēgel, pegel (“level, water guage”); cognate with German Low German Pegel, the noun which has given Standard High German German Pegel (“level, water depth”).

noun:Periode.tx: 15th century as Periodus m or f, a learned borrowing from Latin periodus f, at first in the grammatical sense. The semantic development as well as the form in -e (17th c.) likely under influence of French période.

verb:polieren.tx: From Middle High German polieren, which is borrowed from Old French polir (see modern French polir).

noun:Pottasche.tx: From Pott + Asche, a calque of Dutch potas (older spelling potasch).

noun:Präposition.tx: From Latin praepositio, from praepōnere, equivalent to prä- + Position.

noun:Pheromon.tx: A portmanteau of Ancient Greek φέρω (phérō, “I bring, bear, carry”) + Hormon (“hormone”), coined in 1959 by German chemist Peter Karlson and Swiss zoologist Martin Lüscher.

noun:Präsentation.tx: From präsentieren (“(to) present”) + -ation. For the slideshow sense, compare French présentation, Spanish presentación, Italian presentazione, and Russian презентация (prezentacija).

phrase:Proletarier aller Länder, vereini.tx: This phrase, which comes from Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels' The Communist Manifesto, became one of the most famous rallying cries of communism.

noun:Petrischale.tx: From Petri + Schale. (Named after German bacteriologist Julius Richard Petri (1852–1921).)

noun:Petunie.tx: Learned borrowing from taxonomic name Petunia, from (now obsolete) French pétun (“tobacco”), from Old Tupi petyma (“tobacco”).

noun:Primel.tx: Borrowed (with the vowels reduced post-tonically) from Latin prīmula in the late 18th century, by way of the genus name Primula chosen by Linnaeus due to them being considered one of the first flowers of spring.

verb:plaudern.tx: From Middle High German plūdern (“to rustle, roar”), of onomatopoeic origin; compare Latin blaterare (“to babble”).

noun:Pavian.tx: From Late Middle High German baviān (15th c.), from Middle Dutch baviaen (cf. Modern Dutch baviaan), from older baubijn, from Middle French babouin.

noun:Publikum.tx: Borrowed from Latin pūblicum under influence of French public. First attested in the 18th century.

noun:Pelikan.tx: From Middle High German pellicān, from Latin pelicānus, pelecānus, from Ancient Greek πελεκάν (pelekán).

noun:Popel.tx: 19th century. Said to be of Central German origin. Used for various misshapen or thickish objects.

noun:Polygamie.tx: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πολυγαμία (polugamía), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + γάμος (gámos, “marriage”), equivalent to poly- + -gamie.

noun:Polemik.tx: Borrowed from French polémique, from Ancient Greek πολεμικός (polemikós).

noun:Pfennig.tx: From Middle High German pfennic, from Old High German pfending, from Proto-West Germanic *panning; compare English penny. Doublet of Penunze.

noun:Poesie.tx: Borrowed from French poésie, from Latin poēsis, from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis).

adj:physikalisch.tx: From Latin physicālis. By surface analysis, Physik + -alisch.

noun:Pfurz.tx: From Middle High German vurz, from Old High German furz, from Proto-West Germanic *furtu. Upper German variant of Furz. Compare Bavarian Pfurz.

noun:Pille.tx: From Middle High German pille, from Latin pilula (“little ball”).

verb:packen.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German packen, from Old Saxon *pakko, from Proto-West Germanic *pakkō, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô (“bundle, pack”). Cognate with German Low German packen, Dutch pakken, Saterland Frisian pakje, West Frisian pakke, English pack.

noun:Privileg.tx: From Middle High German prīvilēgje, from Latin prīvilēgium.

adj:passabel.tx: Borrowed from French passable. By surface analysis, passieren + -abel.

adj:prekär.tx: Borrowed from French précaire, from Latin precarius.

noun:Premierminister.tx: Premier + Minister. Partial calque of French premier ministre.

verb:plündern.tx: From Middle High German plundern, plunderen, from Middle Low German plunderen, plünderen, plünren, from Middle Low German plunder, plonder (“robbery, plunder", originally "thing, stuff”), related to Middle Low German plunde, plünde (“junk, stuff, rags, old clothes”), of obscure ultimate origin. This is first attested in medieval records, which according to Gijsseling, is therefore too late to be …

verb:prophezeien.tx: From Middle High German prophēzīen, derived from prophēzīe, a byform of prophētīe (see Prophetie). The z-form was influenced by Old French profecie. The verb itself may also follow Old French profecier (whence at any rate Middle High German prophēzieren).

noun:Pusteblume.tx: Attested 19th century, chiefly from Low German dialects. Analysable as pusten (“to blow”) + Blume (“flower”), from the children’s habit of blowing off the seeds. However, this may be only a remotivation of an underlying dialectal Pissblume, from the dandelion's diuretic effect; compare Dutch pisbloem.

noun:Picknick.tx: Borrowed from French pique-nique or English picnic.

noun:Perfekt.tx: Borrowed from Latin (tempus praeteritum) perfectum (literally “preterite perfect tense”).

verb:patzen.tx: From batzen (“to be soft or sticky; to do surface-level work”), itself from backen (“to stick together; cake”), a sense that derived from the idea of baking.

noun:Politur.tx: From Latin politura; see polieren for more.

noun:Paradigmenwechsel.tx: From Paradigma + -en- + Wechsel, a calque of English paradigm shift.

verb:protestieren.tx: Borrowed from French protester, from Latin prōtestārī, from prō + testor, from testis (“witness”).

noun:Pfefferspray.tx: Calque of English pepper spray; on the surface Pfeffer + Spray, but German Pfeffer means “black pepper”.

noun:Pädagoge.tx: Borrowed from Latin paedagogus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós), from παῖς (paîs, “child”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”).

noun:Pommes.tx: Clipping of Pommes frites with a spelling pronunciation.

adj:pädophil.tx: From Ancient Greek παιδόφιλος (paidóphilos), from παῖς (paîs, “boy, child”) and φιλέω (philéō, “I love”); equivalent to pädo- + -phil.

verb:parlieren.tx: From Middle High German parlieren, from Old French parlier (“to speak”) + -en.

verb:paddeln.tx: Occasionally since circa 1800 from Low German paddeln (“to scurry, tottle, dabble, splash, twitch”), frequentative of padden, padjen (“to step, scurry, walk in shallow water”). Probably from a variant of Middle Low German pedden (“to tread, tramp”), cognate with Dutch pedden, Old English pæþþan, which are considered derivatives of Proto-Germanic *paþaz (“path”); compare also Old High German …

noun:Pantoffel.tx: From Middle High German pantoffel (late 15th century), from Middle French pantoufle (compare French pantoufle) and/or Italian pantofola. Perfect cognate with Dutch pantoffel.

noun:Paparazzo.tx: Borrowed from Italian paparazzo, from the name of a character in Federico Fellini's La dolce vita.

verb:probieren.tx: From Latin probō + -ieren. Doublet of proben and prüfen.

adj:provisorisch.tx: Calque of Medieval Latin provisorius, using Latin provis- (supine stem of provideo) + -orisch (“-ory”).

noun:Predigt.tx: From Middle High German predige, from Old High German prediga, ultimately from Latin praedicō. The -t is unetymological, first appearing in Early New High German, perhaps influenced by Latin praedicātio. Cognate with Hunsrik Pretich.

verb:predigen.tx: From Middle High German predien, predigen, from Old High German predigon, predion, bredigon, which is borrowed from Latin praedicō.

verb:piken.tx: Borrowed from French piquer or denominal from German Pike (“pike”) or both parallelly.

adj:protzig.tx: Protz + -ig, or protzen + -ig, both from the same origin.

verb:pudern.tx: Puder + -n. Possibly a calque of French poudrer.

noun:Präferenz.tx: From French préférence, ultimately from Latin praeferō, praeferre.

adj:prosaisch.tx: Borrowed from French prosaïque, from Medieval Latin prosaicus. By surface analysis, Prosa + -isch.

verb:prägen.tx: From Middle High German præchen/bræchen (“to press in, to depict”), from Old High German giprāhhan/prāhhan (“to press in or scratch by breaking the surface”), from the 1st and 3rd person plural preterite forms of prēchan/prāchun (“to break”); likely related to brechen.

noun:Pferdestärke.tx: From Pferd (“horse”) + -e- + Stärke (“power, strength”), calque of English horsepower.

noun:Prävention.tx: Borrowed from French prévention, from Late Late Latin praeventio, praeventionem, from Latin praeventus, from praevenio.

noun:Pinie.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin pīnea (“pine”), from Latin pīnus (“pine tree”).

noun:Paradiesapfel.tx: From Paradies (“paradise”) + Apfel (“apple”), referring to the fruit of the forbidden tree. Similar forms for “tomato”, perhaps borrowed from German, exist in several eastern European languages; consider Czech rajče.

noun:Provinz.tx: From late Middle High German provincie, from Late Latin provincia (“region, area”), meaning “province, duty, command” in Classical Latin.

noun:Pauke.tx: From Middle High German pūke (“drum”). Further origin unknown, possibly onomatopoeic. Cognate with Yiddish פּויק (poyk).

noun:Partitur.tx: Borrowed from Italian partitura (“partition, musical score”), from Medieval Latin partitūra, from partiō, partior (“to divide, to partition, to share”) + -ūra.

adj:phänomenal.tx: Borrowed from French phénoménal. By surface analysis, Phänomen + -al.

noun:Panther.tx: From Middle High German panter, pantel, from Latin panthera, from Ancient Greek πάνθηρ (pánthēr).

noun:Psychiatrie.tx: Coined by German physician Johann Christian Reil in 1808 (originally in the form Psychiaterie). By surface analysis, psycho- + -iatrie.

noun:Plagiat.tx: Borrowed from French plagiat (“plagiarism”) in the 18th century, from Latin plagiātum.

noun:Planke.tx: From Middle High German (Central German) and Middle Low German planke, both via northern dialects of Old French, planke, ultimately from Late Latin planca, a vulgar variant of phalanga.

noun:Plakat.tx: Borrowed from Dutch plakkaat, from Middle Dutch plakkaert, from French placard.

noun:Pandemie.tx: From Ancient Greek πανδημία (pandēmía, “all the people”)

noun:Pyjama.tx: Borrowed from English pyjamas, from Urdu پایجامه (pāyjāma) and Hindi पैजामा (paijāmā), from Persian پایجامه / پاجامه (pâyjâme / pâjâme, “leg garment”). See پای (pây, "leg") and جامه (jâmeh, garment).

adj:progressiv.tx: Borrowed from French progressif and English progressive, both from Latin prōgressīvus.

verb:pausen.tx: From earlier bausen, a borrowing of French poncer (“to pounce”) influenced by ébaucher (“to sketch”).

noun:Personenschützer.tx: From Person (“person”) + -en- + Schutz (“protection”) + -er (“-er”) or Person + -en- + Schützer.

adj:primär.tx: Early 19th century, from French primaire (thus slightly later than sekundär). Doublet of Premier.

adj:proaktiv.tx: Borrowed from English proactive; analyzable as pro- + aktiv.

noun:Patrone.tx: Borrowed from French patron. The meaning of 'cartridge' developed from 'patron (saint)' > 'pattern' (as in English) > 'standard amount of gunpowder in a case'. Doublet of Patron.

adj:peinlich.tx: From Pein + -lich. Similar to Dutch pijnlijk. Doublet of pingelig.

noun:Pardon.tx: 16th century, from Middle French pardon. The use as an interjection (ca. 1700) after Modern French.

intj:Pardon.tx: 16th century, from Middle French pardon. The use as an interjection (ca. 1700) after Modern French.

noun:Partikel.tx: Borrowed from Latin particula f, diminutive of pars (“part”).

noun:Pein.tx: From Middle High German pīne, from Old High German pīna, from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā (“torment, pain”).

adj:polyglott.tx: 18th century, learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πολύγλωσσος (polúglōssos).

verb:pusten.tx: The modern form is from German Low German pusten, from Middle Low German pûsten, borrowed during the 18th century and spread in this Low German form after that. Ultimately of imitative origin (lautmalend), though it is unclear if the word goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root. Earlier attestations (from the 14th century on) are pausten, pfausten, rarely also pusten. These prove the word to be …

noun:Pädophilie.tx: By surface analysis, pädo- + -philie. Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek παιδοφιλία (paidophilía), from Ancient Greek παῖς (paîs, “boy, child”) + φῐλῐ́ᾱ (phĭlĭ́ā, “love”).

adj:phonetisch.tx: From Ancient Greek φωνητικός (phōnētikós), with assimilation to native suffix -isch.

adj:psychisch.tx: From Psyche + -isch, from Ancient Greek ψυχικός (psukhikós).

adj:pervers.tx: 16th century, from Latin perversus, in part through Middle French pervers.

adj:philosophisch.tx: Probably from Latin philosophicus with -isch for Latin -icus.

noun:Perlmutt.tx: Shortened from now less common Perlmutter, a calque of Latin māter perlārum. The shortening possibly through reinterpretation of perlmuttern as Perlmutt + -ern instead of Perlmutter + -n.

noun:Präteritum.tx: Borrowed from Latin praeteritum, short for tempus praeteritum (literally “having-gone-by time”); the latter is the past participle of praetereō, itself from praeter + eō.

noun:Prothese.tx: From Ancient Greek πρόθεσις (próthesis) and πρόσθεσις (prósthesis).

noun:Präsent.tx: From Middle High German prēsent, prīsant, from Old French present.

noun:Pampers.tx: From English Pampers, a genericized trademark brand of diapers, from English pamper.

noun:Präambel.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin praeambulum, from Latin praeambulō. Compare German preamble.

noun:Pottwal.tx: From Pott + Wal, a calque of Middle Dutch potswal, from Proto-Germanic *puttaz + *hwalaz.

verb:putzen.tx: 15th century, also in the form butzen. Origin unknown. Perhaps derived from Middle High German butze (“lump, piece, stump”), from Old High German *butz, from Proto-West Germanic *butt, from Proto-Germanic *buttaz (whence also English butt), with the interpretation of the verb being "to (remove) lumps and stumps", but there are several other theories. Perhaps related to Latin puto in the sense of "clean".

noun:Pumpernickel.tx: 17th century, from Westphalian Low German Pumpernickel (literally “farting Nicholas”), originally attested in the sense “coarse, clumsy bloke”. From pumpern (“to fart”) + Nickel (diminutive of Nikolaus). The use for the bread alludes to its being coarse-ground and particularly its flatulent effect. It was originally pejorative or at least humorous; the normal Westphalian word is Schwarzbrot (Low German Schwattbraut).

verb:picken.tx: From Middle High German bicken, from Old High German bicken, from Proto-West Germanic *pikkōn, from Proto-Germanic *pikkōną (“to pick, peck, prick, knock”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew-, *bu- (“to make a dull, hollow sound”).

noun:Pfleger.tx: From Middle High German phleger, phlegære, from Old High German phlegāri, from Proto-West Germanic *plegārī. By surface analysis, agent noun of pflegen, equivalent to pflegen + -er.

adj:plausibel.tx: From French plausible, from Latin plausibilis.

noun:Psychoanalyse.tx: Coined by Sigmund Freud, from psycho- (“psycho-”) + Analyse (“analysis”)

noun:Pläne.tx: From Middle High German plān, plāne, from Latin planum, in part through Old French plaine. Secondarily analysable as plan (“level”) + -e (noun-forming suffix). The modern umlaut is based on this reanalysis and/or influenced by Modern French plaine.

noun:Popanz.tx: Borrowed (in the 16th century) from an unidentified Slavic language.

verb:piepen.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German pīpen, from Old Saxon pīpan, from Proto-West Germanic *pīpan (“to squeak”). Doublet of pfeifen.

verb:puffen.tx: From Middle High German buffen, sharing an imitative Proto-Germanic base with Old English pyffan, Middle English puffen, English puff. Compare also Middle Low German puffen, buffen, biffen, German Low German buffen (“to puff”).

noun:Plazenta.tx: Borrowed from Latin placenta. Doublet of Palatschinke.

noun:Paralyse.tx: From Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis).

noun:Praktikum.tx: From the neuter of Late Latin practicus (“practical”), from Ancient Greek πρακτικός (praktikós, “of or pertaining to action, concerned with action or business, active, practical”), from πράσσω (prássō, “I do”).

noun:Pferch.tx: From Middle High German pferrich, from Old High German pherrich (“fence, enclosure”), from Proto-West Germanic *parrik (“fence, enclosure”). Akin to Old English pearruc (“enclosure, paddock, fence”), Old Norse parrak (“enclosure, pond”), Old French parc. German Park is a doublet. See English park and paddock for more.

adj:pompös.tx: From French pompeux, equivalent to Pomp + -ös.

noun:Posten.tx: Borrowed in the 17th century from Italian posto, beginning in military use.

noun:Pater.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin pater. Doublet of Vater.

verb:proben.tx: From Middle High German prōben, from Latin probare (“to test”). Doublet of probieren and prüfen.

verb:platzieren.tx: From French placer + -ieren. Reform spelling reanalysed it as Platz (“place”) + -ieren.

verb:pfropfen.tx: From Middle High German phrophen, from Old High German phrophōn, derived from phropha, from Latin propago.

noun:Partie.tx: Borrowed from French partie. Doublet of Partei and Party.

verb:pressen.tx: From Middle High German pressen, from Old High German pressōn, from Latin pressō. Doublet of pressieren.

noun:Permanenz.tx: From Medieval Latin permanentia, from Latin permaneō (“to remain; last”).

noun:Pharisäer.tx: The name of the coffee drink is a reference to the veiled consumption of alcohol.

noun:Polynom.tx: From poly- + -nom, from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós).

noun:Purpur.tx: From Old High German purpura, from Proto-West Germanic *purpurā (“purple”).

noun:Politbüro.tx: Borrowed from Russian Политбюро (Politbjuro), reinforced by German Büro. Analysable as polit- (“political”) + Büro (“office”).

adj:produktiv.tx: Borrowed from French productif, from Latin prōdūcō.

adj:primitiv.tx: From Latin prīmitīvus, via French primitif.

verb:pauken.tx: Derived from Middle High German pūken (“to beat, brawl”), probably ultimately related to Pauker (“teacher”), compare also German Pauke (“kettledrum”).

noun:Posse.tx: Clipping of Possenspiel (Possen (“joke; farce”) + Spiel (“game, play”)).

noun:Possen.tx: From Middle High German posse (“prank, farce”), from Old French bosse (“bump, lump, swelling, sublimity, loftiness”), from Vulgar Latin *bottia, from Frankish *bottija, from Frankish *bōtan (“to strike, knock down”), from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to beat, push”).

verb:pochen.tx: From Middle High German bochen, puchen, from Proto-Germanic *puk-, which is probably imitative. Or, perhaps related to French poquer (“move in pétanque”).

noun:Pokémon.tx: Borrowed from Japanese ポケモン (Pokemon), a contraction of ポケットモンスター (Poketto Monsutā), itself from English pocket monster.

noun:Papp.tx: From late Middle High German *pappe (“pap, mash”). The noun is attested in the 15th century, but compare the derivative pepelen (“to feed, foster”, modern päppeln) in the 13th century. According to Frings, who considered it originally Rhenish, ultimately a borrowing from Latin pappa (“word called by infants for food”). However, independent origin in onomatopoeia and baby-talk (Lallwort) is now …

verb:parkieren.tx: Either borrowed from French parquer or formed analogously to it from Park + -ieren. Equivalent to Alemannic German parkiere.

noun:Police.tx: Borrowed from French police, from Italian polizza. Doublet of Polizze.

intj:Pustekuchen.tx: Early 20th century, originally Berlin slang. By surface analysis, pusten (“to blow”) + Kuchen (“cake, pie”). The word Kuchen on its own is already attested with the same sense in thieves' cant (Rotwelsch) since 1818, and likely goes back to Yiddish חכם (khokhem, “wise or cunning man”), used here with a sense along the lines of “you wise guy!” or “you trickster!”. The first component may be …

noun:Pulk.tx: Borrowed from Polish pułk, from Proto-Slavic *pъlkъ, probably from Proto-Germanic *fulką, and then a doublet of Volk.

noun:Prosopagnosie.tx: Ancient Greek πρόσωπον (prósōpon, “face”) + Agnosie (“agnosia”), from Ancient Greek ἀγνωσία (agnōsía). Apparently coined by neurologist Joachim Bodamer in 1947 in a paper describing the condition, titled Die Prosop-Agnosie.

noun:Pipe.tx: Borrowed from Italian pipa, from Vulgar Latin *pīpa. Compare Bavarian Pipn.

adj:perniziös.tx: Borrowed from French pernicieux, from Latin perniciōsus.

noun:Piranha.tx: From Portuguese piranha, from Old Tupi pirãîa.

noun:Port.tx: From Middle High German port, borrowed from Old French port, itself borrowed from Latin portus (“harbor”).

noun:Piks.tx: From piksen (“to prick, to sting, to pinch”), also piken.

noun:Pakt.tx: From Latin pactum (“something agreed upon”), from paciscere (“to agree”). Cognate with English pact.

noun:Pott.tx: From Middle Low German pot and Middle High German pot (West Central German, 12th century), from Old Saxon *pott, from Proto-West Germanic *pott, from Proto-Germanic *puttaz. See English pot for more.

noun:Psilocybin.tx: Psilocybe + -in. Coined by Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann, after translingual Psilocybe, from New Latin psīlocybē, from Ancient Greek ψιλός (psilós, “smooth”) + κύβη (kúbē, “head”).

adj:punktuell.tx: Ultimately from Late Latin pūnctuālis, possibly through French ponctuel with the vocalism realigned with Punkt.

noun:Polier.tx: From Early New High German parlier, from Middle High German parlier, parlierer, related to parlieren.

noun:Pfriem.tx: From Middle High German pfrieme, from Proto-Germanic *preumaz (compare Low German Preen, Dutch priem), alteration of *preunaz, from Proto-Indo-European *brewn- (compare Lithuanian briaunà (“edge”), Albanian brez (“belt, girdle”)). See English preen for reference.

noun:Pekannuss.tx: From Pekan + Nuss, borrowed from English pecan, from French pacane, ultimately of Algonquian origin.

noun:Pedelec.tx: Blend of pedal + electric + cycle, coined by Susanne Brüsch in 1999.

verb:präsentieren.tx: Inherited from Middle High German prēsentieren, borrowed from Old French présenter. Cognate with French présenter.

noun:Panel.tx: Borrowed from English panel. Doublet of Paneel.

noun:Parka.tx: Borrowed from English parka, from Aleut parka, from Russian па́рка (párka).

noun:Pingo.tx: Via English pingo from Greenlandic pingu or Inuktitut pingu (“small hill”).

noun:Packen.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German packe, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô.

adj:putzig.tx: Borrowed from Low German or Dutch potsig (“funny, cute”), which belongs to Old French bocer.; related to Butz (“goblin”).

noun:Pöbel.tx: From Middle High German povel, bovel (“folk, people”, ca. 1200). Generally derived from Old French pueble, pueple. However, since Middle High German consistently shows -v-, borrowing from Italian Gallo-Romance povolo should also be considered. In any case from Latin populus. The form with -b- shows a later, chiefly East Central German development and was spread by Luther’s Bible. The umlaut is …

verb:preisgeben.tx: Ca. 1600, from Preise (“prize, booty”) + geben (“to give”), thus originally “to surrender as enemy booty”. Preise is an obsolete form of Prise, which see. Compare Dutch prijsgeven.

noun:Palas.tx: Learned borrowing from Middle High German palas, from Old French palais, pales, from Late Latin palātium. Doublet of Pfalz, Palast, and Palais.

noun:Performance.tx: Borrowed from English performance. Doublet of Performanz.

noun:Podium.tx: From Latin podium, from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “foot of vase”), diminutive of πούς (poús, “foot”).

noun:Platt.tx: Ultimately the same as platt (“flat”), although the motivation seems not to be quite clear; possibly the geographically low areas of Germany as in Niederdeutsch (“Low German”), or else “not elevated, ordinary, simple” speech. Cognate to Dutch plat n (“dialect”), Central Franconian Platt (“dialect”), Low German Platt n (“Low German”)

noun:Pohl.tx: Dialectal form of standard Pfahl, used in this form in most dialects of North Rhine-Westphalia, including German Low German [Term?], Low Franconian, and Ripuarian. Cognate with Limburgish paol, Luxembourgish Poul, Dutch paal, and English pole.

noun:Pfuhl.tx: From Middle High German pfuol, from Old High German pfuol, from Proto-West Germanic *pōl, from Proto-Germanic *pōlaz. Akin to English pool and Dutch poel.

verb:preisen.tx: From Middle High German prīsen (“to praise”), a derivative of the noun prīs (“prize”) (whence modern German Preis), influenced by Old French prisier (“to appraise, value”), from Late Latin pretiō (“to esteem, value”).

noun:Putz.tx: Related to putzen, unknown as for its derivation beyond German. * perhaps related to Batzen (“clump as shaped to the hand”) also of unknown etymology * perhaps onomatopoeia, like Batzen * perhaps putzen is a causative form of besser, as in older language and dialects the beginning consonant is often ⟨b⟩.

noun:Pleonasmus.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós, “abundance; excess”).

verb:prasseln.tx: From Middle High German brasteln, iterative intensive formation from brasten, from Old High German brastōn (“to roar, crash”), ultimately from the root of bersten (“to burst”).

noun:Paniermehl.tx: From panieren (“to bread, to crumb”) + Mehl (“flour”).

noun:Patella.tx: Borrowed from Latin patella (“a small pan or dish, a plate; the kneepan, patella”), diminutive of patina (“a broad shallow dish, pan”).

noun:Pauschale.tx: Austrian officialese from Southern German Pausch, Bausch (“wad”), which occurs primarily in the phrase in Bausch und Bogen (“taken as a whole, completely”). Originally neuter, with a change of gender occurring in the 20th century, but the original gender is still retained in officialese language.

noun:Prunk.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German prunk, probably related to the root of prangen (“to show off”).

noun:Priorat.tx: Borrowed from Latin priōrātus. By surface analysis, Prior + -at.

noun:Produktionsmittel.tx: Produktion + -s- + Mittel. Coined by German-born philosopher Karl Marx.

noun:Puszta.tx: Borrowed from Hungarian puszta. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *pustъ.

noun:Penne.tx: Corruption of Pennal, influenced by etymology 2.

noun:Pfaffe.tx: From Middle High German pfaffe, from Old High German pfaffo, phaffo, an early borrowing from Gothic 𐍀𐌰𐍀𐌰 (papa) demonstrating the effects of the High German consonant shift, from Ancient Greek πάπας (pápas). Cognate to Dutch paap. Doublet of Papst.

adj:pedantisch.tx: Pedant + -isch, likely a calque of French pédantesque, itself derived from Italian pedantesco.

noun:Polder.tx: Borrowed in the 18th century from Dutch polder, from Middle Dutch polre, from Old Dutch *polra (attested as polre in a Latin text). Further origin unknown.

noun:Pillepalle.tx: Reduplication with ablaut of dialectal (Rhinelandic) Pill (“something small”), perhaps from Latin pilula (“pill”). See Klein-Klein for a similar construction.

noun:Pausbacke.tx: * The word is documented since the 16th century. It is a compound formed with the noun Backe and the stem of an obsolete verb whose (West Central German) Late Middle High German form was pūsen (see pusten) and whose Early New High German equivalent was pausen, bausen ‘to be blown-up; to billow, to distend; to swell; to be full of, to be bursting with’. In Early New High German these forms were …

noun:Pirsch.tx: An abstract noun and back-formation from pirschen; its Early New High German form was Birs, from Middle High German birse and berse.

noun:Pastete.tx: Inherited from Middle High German pastēde, likely from Middle Dutch pasteide, from Old French pasté, from Late Latin pasta (“paste, dough, pastry cake”). See there for more. Cognate with Hunsrik Pasdet.

noun:Postskriptum.tx: Borrowed from Latin postscrīptum, from postscrībō (“I write after”).

verb:poltern.tx: Onomatopoeic, from Middle High German buldern, from Middle Low German bolderen. Compare Polish pultać.

noun:Pirol.tx: From Middle High German piro, ultimately from Ancient Greek πῠρρός (pŭrrhós, “tawny”).

noun:Pimpf.tx: From earlier Pumpf (literally “little fart”). See also pumpernickel.

verb:plärren.tx: From Middle High German blēren, blerren. Comparable and possibly cognate with Dutch blaren, whence English blare. Eventually of onomatopoeic origin.

adj:pingelig.tx: From Ripuarian Central Franconian pengelig, pingelig and Low Franconian, in Ripuarian derived from Peng, Ping (“pain”), originally in the sense of German wehleidig (“over-sensitive, whiny”). Formally a doublet of standard peinlich (“hurtful; embarrassing”).

verb:plumpsen.tx: From plumpen + -sen, the former from Middle Low German plumpen (“to fall heavily”). See plump for more.

noun:Pore.tx: Borrowed from Latin porus. Pfeifer explains the change in gender as a backformation of the plural Poren in the second half of 18th century. Kluge says it was borrowed in the 15th century, presumably referring to earlier plural use.

noun:Palaver.tx: From English palaver. Doublet of Parabel and Parole. Associated with native labern (“to chatter, babble”), whence the informal alternative pronunciation.

verb:prangen.tx: From Middle High German prangen, brangen, probably ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *brahtaz, whence Pracht (“splendor”).

noun:Pfründe.tx: From Middle High German pfrüende, pfruonde, from Old High German phruonta, from (early) Medieval Latin provenda, alteration of Latin praebenda.

noun:Prämie.tx: Borrowed from Latin praemia, derived from praemium.

noun:Pluderhose.tx: From pludern (“to be baggy; bunch up”) + Hose (“trouser”).

noun:Plagiator.tx: Borrowed from Latin plagiātor, from Latin plagiō + -tor, with a semantic shift; compare German Plagiat.

adj:prall.tx: From Low German pral, from Middle Low German pral (literally “to bounce, spring back”), ultimately related to prallen (“to collide”).

noun:Poulet.tx: Borrowed from French poulet, from poule + -et.

noun:Passat.tx: Borrowed from Dutch passaat via Low German.

noun:Pegel.tx: Borrowed from Low German Pegel, from Middle Low German pēgel, from Proto-West Germanic *pagil. Cognate with English pail.

noun:Pulle.tx: Borrowed from Low German Pull(e), from Middle Low German appulle, from Latin ampulla. Doublet of Ampel and Ampulle. Compare Dutch pul (“tankard”).

noun:Phiole.tx: From Middle High German viole, from Medieval Latin fiola, from phiala. Doublet of Fiale.

noun:Pneumonie.tx: From Ancient Greek πνευμονία (pneumonía, “lung disease”), from πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”) + -ία (-ía).

noun:Pumps.tx: Borrowed from English pumps, plural of pump. Further origin unsettled.

noun:Propst.tx: From Middle High German prob(e)st, brobest, from Old High German probost, probist, provost, from Old French provost, from Latin praepositus.

noun:Pick.tx: Denominal of picken in the sense “to adhere”.

verb:prallen.tx: From Middle High German prellen (“to bash, bruise”), which see. Compare Middle Low German prallen, prellen, brallen (“to collide, bump, crash”), whence German Low German prallen.

adj:palliativ.tx: From Medieval Latin palliātīvus, from Latin palliō (“I conceal”).

adj:patriarchalisch.tx: Blend of patriarchal + patriarchisch, or simply from patriarchal + -isch. The three forms remain widely synonymous, though patriarchisch is more often said of people, while patriarchal(isch) is said of societies, etc.

adj:picobello.tx: Pseudo-Italianism; humorous alteration of piekfein with fein replaced by Italian bello.

adj:piekfein.tx: From Low German püükfien, tautological compound of püük + fien, both roughly “excellent, fine, clean, honest”. The former is a borrowing from Dutch puik, from Middle Dutch puuc, from Old Dutch *puiken, from Proto-West Germanic *pūka, *pūga, from Pre-Germanic *pūkk, of uncertain origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European *buk-, *bu-, *beu- (“to blow, swell”), assuming an original sense of "bag made from …

adj:possessiv.tx: Borrowed from Latin possessīvus (“of or pertaining to possession”), from possideō (“to possess”).

adj:praktikabel.tx: Borrowed from French practicable, from Medieval Latin practicabilis.

noun:Platzregen.tx: Late 15th century, from platz(en) + Regen (“rain”). The verb is used here in its original sense “to splat, fall noisily”, for which otherwise now the variant platschen.

adj:prämiert.tx: From Latin praemia, plural of praemium (“prize, reward”).

noun:Plötze.tx: From Middle Low German plötze (14th c.), from Polabian and/or Old Polish (cf. modern Polish płoć, płotka). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *plotь.

noun:Pädophiler.tx: From the substantivisation of pädophil (“paedophile / pedophile (adj)”).

noun:Pferdeapfel.tx: Pferd + Apfel. Probably with reference to the supposed similarity to rotten apples.

verb:prassen.tx: Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German brassen, probably related to the root of Swedish brasa (“small fire”), French braise (“live coals”), comparing boastful behavior to the sound of roasting food.

noun:Polente.tx: Rotwelsch (thieves' cant), variation of Polizei, 19th c.

noun:Piefke.tx: From the Prussian composer of military music Johann Gottfried Piefke.

noun:Protz.tx: Perhaps from regional terms for toad, from Middle High German broȥȥen (“to swell”), just as braggarts inflate themselves with their pride and ego. Further origin is uncertain; speculative connections have been made to Proto-Indo-European *bʰrews- (“to swell”), whence Proto-Germanic *breustą (“breast, chest”).

noun:Plörre.tx: From German Low German Plör, Plörre, probably from the verb plören, itself possibly identical with Dutch pleuren and French pleurer. The senses of these verbs are somewhat diffuse. Duden cites “to cry, weep” and “to spill, slop”. For the Dutch verb, “to fling, hurl”, “to fall, collapse”, “to rot, decay”, and “to rain hard” are mentioned. The original sense of Plörre may thus be that of stale …

noun:Pfeffersack.tx: Pfeffer + Sack, originally referring to the owners of ships carrying (then valuable) pepper and other spices.

verb:plattmachen.tx: From platt + machen; cognate with Hunsrik plattmache.

verb:petzen.tx: Uncertain. Attested since the end of the 18th century, emerged in Halle, Germany, spread to all major German university cities by mid-19th century. Perhaps from Rotwelsch petzen, pezetten (“to report to the police, to betray”), from Yiddish [script needed] (Pezet), [script needed] (Peizaddik, “police”), from [script needed] (pe, “p (letter name)”) + [script needed] (zadik, “z (letter name)”) …

noun:Petze.tx: Back-formation from petzen; see there for more. Since the end of the 19th century.

noun:Peperoni.tx: Borrowed from Italian peperoni, plural of peperone (“bell pepper”).

verb:pfuschen.tx: Possibly from futsch, itself probably onomatopoeic.
