noun:Privatier.tx: From privat + -ier after Rentier, itself from French rentier.

noun:Peanuts.tx: Borrowed from English peanuts. Popularized by former Deutsche Bank chairman Hilmar Kopper who used the word to describe a sum of 50 million DM (c. 25 million €).

noun:Paneel.tx: From Middle Low German panēl, probably through Middle Dutch paneel eventually from Old French panel, from Vulgar Latin *pannellus. Doublet of Panel.

noun:Palstek.tx: From Low German, from Middle Low German pâl (“stake, post”) + stēke (“stitch, knot”), equivalent to standard German Pfahl + Stich. Compare Dutch paalsteek.

noun:Piñata.tx: Borrowed from Spanish piñata, from Italian pignatta (“pot”), from Italian pigna (“pine cone”), from Latin pīnea.

noun:Pirogge.tx: Chiefly from Russian пирог (pirog). Reinforced by Polish pieróg. First attestations in the 17th century, more regular use since the 19th century.

noun:Pranke.tx: From Middle High German pranke, a Romance borrowing, found as Late Latin branca, from Gaulish.

noun:Panier.tx: From older Banier, from Middle High German banier, baniere, borrowed from Old French baniere, itself from Frankish [Term?]. Doublet of Banner.

noun:Polohemd.tx: Calque of English polo shirt; Polo + Hemd

verb:preschen.tx: Ultimately equivalent to pirschen (“to stalk while hunting”) with metathesis and a shift in semantics from hunting towards fast movement.

noun:Promoter.tx: Borrowed from English promoter. Doublet of Promotor.

noun:Poliklinik.tx: Earlier 19th century, coined from Ancient Greek πόλις (pólis, “town, city”) + Klinik.

verb:plätten.tx: 18th century, from Low and Central German dialects, ultimately from Middle Low German pletten (“to flatten, smooth”). Cognate with Dutch pletten. By surface analysis, platt + -en.

pt: to prick, to sting, to pinch
verb:piksen.tx: piken (“to prick, to sting, to pinch”) + -sen (“intensive suffix”).

noun:Pervitin.tx: Marketing coinage, introduced 1938 by Temmler Werke (discontinued 1988).

noun:Preuße.tx: From Middle High German Priuze, from Old Prussian *Prūsas.

noun:Piment.tx: Borrowed from French piment, from Spanish pimiento, from Latin pigmentum, hence doublet of Pigment.

noun:Plaste.tx: From Thermoplaste, plural of Thermoplast (“thermoplastic”), originally a tradename used by Buna Werke Schkopau.

noun:Priel.tx: 18th century, borrowed from Low German Priel, whence also Dutch priel. Further origin unknown.

noun:Part.tx: From Middle High German part f (“share, part, party”), from Old French part, from Latin pars.

noun:Papsttum.tx: From Middle High German bābestuom. Equivalent to Papst + -tum.

noun:Parapluie.tx: Borrowed from French parapluie. Compare Alemannic German Baareblyy, Bavarian Parablü, Central Franconian Paraplü, Luxembourgish Prabbeli.

noun:Polterabend.tx: From poltern + Abend, literally “noisy party”, from the custom of breaking porcelain to bring luck to the couple's marriage.

verb:prellen.tx: From Middle High German prellen (“to hit, push with force, move quickly”), of obscure ultimate origin, but perhaps imitative.

noun:Pädiatrie.tx: Borrowed from English pediatrics, equivalent to pädo- (“pedo-”) + -iatrie (“-iatry”).

verb:panschen.tx: 18th century (in compounds since 15th century). Origin uncertain. Probably onomatopoeic, compare patschen and manschen.

noun:Pomelo.tx: Borrowed from English pomelo. Doublet of Pampelmuse.

noun:Pferdekuss.tx: From Pferd (“horse”) + Kuss (“kiss”). Derived from the dated humorous idiomatic expression vom Pferd geküsst werden (literally “to get kissed by a horse”), which first applied the sense of "to get bitten by a horse", then also of "to get kicked by a horse".

noun:Pfefferminze.tx: From Pfeffer (“pepper”) + Minze (“mint”). Compare English peppermint.

noun:Pocke.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German pocke, from Proto-Germanic *puhô. Cognate with Dutch pok, English pock. Displaced the variants Poche, Pfoche, which may go back to related Proto-Germanic *puhô, but are perhaps merely inadequate adaptations of the Low German form. The native High German word for “pock” is Blatter.

noun:Protze.tx: Borrowed from Italian biroccio, from Late Latin *birotium, from Latin birotus (“two-wheeled”).

noun:Pritsche.tx: From Middle High German *britze (attested in derivatives, simplex 15th c.), from Old High German britissa (“thin plank”), derived from bret (Proto-Germanic *bredą, whence modern Brett) + -issa (Proto-Germanic *-isjō). P- for initial b- and -tsch- for -tz- are sporadic developments, here reinforced by onomatopoeia. The predominant sense in older Modern German was that of a baton.

verb:päppeln.tx: From Middle High German pepelen, *peppelen, derived from *pappe (“pap, flour mash”). See Papp.

noun:Pappenstiel.tx: In a lost unfigurative sense the worthless bare stalk of a certain plant, * either the ubiquitous dandelion also named Pfaffenplume, Low German Pappenblome, * or, as in the 16th century where this idiom is also is from, Rübenstiel has been used in this sense, Low German Piepe (“turnip”) whence pfeifen auf etw., es ist mir piepe, piepegal if that is not instead from the bird-imitating piep, * or …

verb:patschen.tx: Onomatopoeic. Derived from the interjection patsch. See platschen, klatschen and bumsen.

noun:Peschmerga.tx: Borrowed from Central Kurdish پێشمەرگە (pêşmerge). The use of -a for the final vowel is probably influenced by other European languages (including English) where this is done to avoid a fronted pronunciation of the letter -g-. The Kurdish vowel is the same in the last two syllables (phonetically [æ]).

noun:Pastinake.tx: From Middle High German pasternacke, from Old High German pastinaka, from Proto-West Germanic *pastinakā (“parsnip”).

noun:Professur.tx: Professor + -ur with a clipping of the -or-

noun:Pfuscher.tx: From pfuschen (“to botch, to work unprofessionally”) + -er (agent suffix).

noun:Pips.tx: A West Central German form, which displaced the more southeastern variants above. From Middle High German pippis, phiphiz, from Old High German pipz, phiphiz, phiffiz, early borrowing from Vulgar Latin pip(p)ita, alteration of Latin pituita. Cognate with Dutch pip, English pip, French pépie.

noun:Pamphlet.tx: Borrowed from French pamphlet, from English pamphlet.

verb:pirschen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German birsen, from Old French berser.

noun:Priem.tx: From Dutch pruim (piece of chewing tobacco).

noun:Praliné.tx: Derived from French praliné, past participle of praliner (“to coat”).

intj:pardauz.tx: From Low German pardu(t)z, from Middle Low German pardûs, ultimately onomatopoeic. The form with -au- occurs first in Campe’s writings and might be a mechanical adaptation to the Standard German vocalism. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål bardus, Dutch pardoes, perdoes, Swedish burdus, and Danish bardus.

noun:Pinke.tx: Perhaps related to Penunze and/or onomatopoeic.

noun:Popstar.tx: Borrowed from English pop star, equivalent to Pop (“pop”) + Star (“star”).

noun:Pfefferkuchen.tx: Pfeffer (“pepper”) + Kuchen (“cake”). Compare Dutch peperkoek, Danish peberkage, Norwegian Bokmål pepperkake, Norwegian Nynorsk peparkake, Swedish pepparkaka.

noun:Poetik.tx: Borrowed from French poétique, from Latin poētica, from Ancient Greek ποιητικός (poiētikós).

noun:Protokollant.tx: 19th century, from protokoll-, stem of protokollieren, + -ant.

verb:polstern.tx: Polster + -en, since the end of the 18th century.

verb:pökeln.tx: From Pökel m (“brine”) + -en, from Middle Low German pekel f (“brine”). Ultimately perhaps from Latin *picco (“to sting”). Compare English pickle.

noun:Pütz.tx: From West Central German, from northern Middle High German pütze, from Old High German putzi, from Proto-West Germanic *puti (“a well”). Doublet of Pfütze (“puddle”) and Pütt (“mine shaft”).

noun:Pinkel.tx: Borrowed from Low German Pinkel, perhaps from Pink (“pinkie, penis”); compare Dutch pink.

noun:Präser.tx: Clipping of Präservativ with change of gender.

noun:Protoplasma.tx: Coined by Czech physiologist Jan Evangelista Purkyně.

noun:Pappenheimer.tx: From Pappenheim + -er. Figurative sense from a well-known line in the play Walleinstein's Death (1799).

noun:Popmusik.tx: Partial calque of English pop music, equivalent to Pop + Musik.

noun:Pflichtteil.tx: From Pflicht (“obligation”) + Teil (“portion, share”). Regularly the word should be only masculine as the sense “portion” is otherwise always masculine, but the neuter is also common.

verb:planieren.tx: French planer, by surface analysis, plan + -ieren

noun:Praller.tx: Either prallen + -er or a clipping of Pralltriller.

verb:purzeln.tx: Inherited from Middle High German purzeln, pürzeln, burzeln, iterative of burzen (“to fall over”). Related to Bürzel, which preserved the original consonantism.

noun:Probiotikum.tx: pro- + Ancient Greek βιωτικός (biōtikós), from Ancient Greek βίος (bíos, “life”).

noun:Phänotyp.tx: Originally coined in German as Phaenotypus by Danish geneticist Wilhelm Johannsen in 1909, ultimately from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, to show, to appear”) + τύπος (túpos, “mark, type”).

noun:Pissnelke.tx: Shitgibbon compound of pissen (“to piss”) + Nelke (“carnation”).

noun:Pfalzgraf.tx: From Middle High German phalenzgrâve. Analyzable as Pfalz + Graf.

noun:Piepmatz.tx: From piepen (“to cheep”) + Matz (short form of Matthias, Matthäus).

phrase:panta rhei.tx: Unadapted borrowing from Ancient Greek πάντα ῥεῖ (pánta rheî, “everything flows”), coined by Ancient Greek philosopher Heraclitus.

verb:parodieren.tx: From French parodie + -ieren, from Latin parōdia, from Ancient Greek παρῳδία (parōidía).

noun:Pauker.tx: Inherited from Middle High German pūkære. The sense of "teacher" is attested since 18th century, shortened from Arschpauker (literally “someone who beats the bottom when teaching”), equivalent to arsch- (“intensifier”) + Pauke (“kettledrum”).

verb:plustern.tx: Ca. 1600, from Middle Low German plûsteren, iterative of plûsen (“to pick, pluck”). The sense developed from the way that chickens and other poultry groom their plumage. Cognate with Middle Dutch plûusteren; compare also Modern Dutch pluizen. Further origin uncertain; possibly from Old French peluchier.

noun:Puste.tx: German Low German, related to pusten.

noun:Pedell.tx: Middle High German pedel, from Medieval Latin pedellus, bedellus, perhaps influenced by Büttel, from Proto-Germanic *budilaz. Cognate with English bedel and beadle.

adj:preziös.tx: Borrowed from French précieux or directly from Latin pretiōsus.

verb:prompten.tx: Borrowed from English prompt or from Prompt + -en.

noun:Patronenhülse.tx: Compound of Patrone (“cartridge, round”) + -n- + Hülse (“hull, casing”).

noun:Proll.tx: After 1950, short for Prolet, itself from Proletarier.

noun:Pilzkopf.tx: Compound of Pilz + Kopf, literally “mushroom head”.

noun:Pülcher.tx: From Bavarian Pülcher, from Middle High German pilgerīn, bilgerīn, bilgerīm, from Old High German piligrīm, from Proto-West Germanic *pelegrīm (“pilgrim, foreigner”). Doublet of Pilger.

noun:Plumpsack.tx: From Latin plumbum swapped with plump (“plump, clumsy”) or plumpsen (“to plump”) and Klump(e) (“lump”) + Sack (“bag”).

noun:Pickert.tx: Probably from Low German Pick, Piäk (“pitch”) + -ert (noun-forming suffix). Compare Westphalian picken, piäken (“to stick”), northern German pekig (“covered in sticky dirt”). It is conspicuous that the vowel of Pickert, unlike that of the aforementioned words, is short in all dialects. However, this may be due to the shortening effect that following -er- commonly has in Low German.

noun:Pole-Position.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English pole position

verb:pflichten.tx: From Middle High German phlihten, derived from the noun phliht, phlihte, from Old High German phliht. By surface analysis, Pflicht + -en.

noun:Palankin.tx: From French palanquin, from Portuguese palanquim (“palanquin, palanquin-bearer”), from Odia ପାଲଙ୍କି (pālaṅki, “litter”), ultimately from Sanskrit पल्यङ्क (palyaṅka), variant of पर्यङ्क (paryaṅka, “bed, couch, litter”).

noun:Privatjet.tx: privat + Jet, calque of English private jet.

verb:pladdern.tx: From Low German pladdern, with shortening before -er- (as e.g. in verheddern) from Middle Low German plāderen. Cognate with Middle Dutch pladeren (dialectal Dutch plaaieren, plaren). Ultimately of onomatopoeic origin; compare plätschern, prasseln.

noun:Plockwurst.tx: From Low German Plockwost. For the first element there are three explanations: (1) from Middle Low German plock, pluck (“post, stake”), cognate of German Pflock, due to its shape, which is reminiscent of a fence post; (2) from a variant of Block (“block”); (3) from a Low German word for “lump of fat”, in turn likely from Middle Low German plücken (“to pluck”), cognate of German pflücken; perhaps …

noun:Preis-Leistungs-Verhältnis.tx: From Preis (“price”) + Leistung (“performance”) + -s- (linking interfix) + Verhältnis (“ratio”). Calque of English price-performance ratio.

noun:Paper.tx: Borrowed from English paper. Doublet of Papier and Papyrus.

noun:Portfolio.tx: Borrowed from English portfolio. Doublet of Portefeuille.

noun:Persilschein.tx: Compound of Persil (“a brand of laundry detergent”) + Schein (“ticket, document”) with the implication of "washing oneself clean (of association)".

noun:Publicity.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English publicity. Doublet of publik, Publikation, Publikum, and Publizität.

noun:Plexus.tx: Borrowed from Latin plexus (“braided”), from plectere.

noun:Psalter.tx: From Middle High German salter, from Old High German saltāri, from Latin psaltērium, from Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion). The modern Ps- is due to relatinization; see Psalm for more.

verb:photoshoppen.tx: Borrowed from English photoshop, influenced by shoppen.

noun:Pelargonie.tx: From the genus name, translingual Pelargonium.

noun:Philatelist.tx: Borrowed from French philatéliste. Analyzable as Philatelie + -ist (agent noun suffix).

noun:Proklamation.tx: Borrowed from French proclamation, from Late Latin prōclāmātiō.

noun:Plattwurm.tx: By surface analysis, platt (“flat”) + Wurm (“worm”). Compare English flatworm, translingual Platyhelminthes.

intj:pfau.tx: Exclamatory. Not related to the noun Pfau.

noun:Prompt.tx: Borrowed from English prompt. Doublet of prompt.

noun:Podcaster.tx: Borrowed from English podcaster or from Podcast + -er.

intj:prösterchen.tx: From prost (“cheers”) + -er- + -chen (diminutive suffix). Interfixing of -er- in diminutives is rare, but not without example; cf. Hüsterchen.

noun:Pummel.tx: Uncertain. Perhaps ultimately onomatopoeic. Compare German Bommel (“bobble”), German Low German Pumpel.

noun:Pfarre.tx: Inherited from Middle High German pharre, Old High German pharra.

noun:Perversion.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin perversiōnis. By surface analysis, pervers + -ion.

noun:Pilaw.tx: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پلاو (pilav), from Classical Persian پلاو (pilāw).

noun:Plopp.tx: Derived from the verb ploppen (“to to make a popping or plopping sound”).

noun:Palliativ.tx: From Medieval Latin palliātīvum, neuter singular form of palliātīvus, from Latin palliō (“I conceal”).

noun:Pygmäe.tx: From Latin Pygmaeī, from Ancient Greek πυγμαῖος (pugmaîos, “a member of a race of dwarves”), from πυγμή (pugmḗ, “fist (as small as a fist)”).

noun:Persimone.tx: Borrowed from English persimmon, from Powhatan pasimenan (“dried fruit”).
